claims.text: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and is brittle.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause the limited tensile ductility and brittleness of the untreated alloy.
A sub-solvus post-solidification aging treatment can induce fine coherent precipitates selectively at lamellar interfaces or colony boundaries.
The targeted structural mediator is a population of nanoscale coherent precipitates at lamellar colony boundaries.
Boundary precipitates would act as interfacial reinforcements and disrupt otherwise continuous internal boundaries.
Boundary precipitates would reduce the effective length available for dislocation pile-ups.
Boundary precipitates would promote more uniform dislocation transmission across lamellar colonies.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups would reduce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic tensile damage.
Particle reinforcement can maintain or enhance the alloy's load-bearing capacity.
The aging treatment will increase room-temperature tensile strain-to-failure relative to the untreated alloy.
The aging treatment will retain or increase strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment's benefit is sensitive to aging temperature and duration.
Over-aging may coarsen the precipitates or strengthen interfaces excessively and thereby reintroduce brittleness.
The treatment outcome may depend on subtle compositional variations in the eutectic alloy.
Precipitate-induced interruption of dislocation accumulation is well established in similar multiphase alloys.
Room-temperature tensile testing and TEM/SEM characterization are proposed to compare aged and untreated specimens from the same batch.
